nameStory: The 'button' in button lichen refers to the small, round fruiting bodies (called apothecia) that look like tiny dark buttons scattered across the lichen's surface. The species name 'griseovirens' comes from Latin meaning 'gray-green,' describing its subtle coloration that shifts between these two tones depending on moisture and light conditions.
description: Buellia griseovirens is a crustose lichen that forms thin, crusty patches directly on tree bark and wooden surfaces. Like all lichens, it's actually a partnership between a fungus and algae working together as one organism. This particular button lichen creates flat, somewhat circular patches that can range from gray to greenish-gray, with small dark fruiting bodies dotting the surface like tiny buttons.

idTips.label: Growth form
idTips.description: Forms thin, crusty patches that feel rough and slightly gritty to the touch, growing directly on the bark surface without any leafy or branching structures

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Gray to greenish-gray overall, often appearing more greenish when damp and grayer when dry

idTips.label: Fruiting bodies
idTips.description: Small, dark, round apothecia (fruiting bodies) scattered across the surface like tiny black or dark brown buttons

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Surface feels slightly rough and granular, not smooth or powdery like some other crusty lichens

idTips.label: Substrate preference
idTips.description: Found on smooth bark of living trees and worked timber, preferring well-lit locations rather than deep shade

habitat: Look for this lichen on the smooth bark of deciduous and coniferous trees in well-lit areas throughout New England's forests, parks, and suburban areas. It particularly favors trees with relatively smooth bark and can also be found on wooden structures like fences, decks, and buildings. This species tolerates moderate air pollution, so you might spot it even in more developed areas where other lichens struggle.

seasonality.spring: Lichen patches may appear slightly more greenish as spring moisture activates the algal partner. This is a good time to spot the contrast between the gray lichen body and dark fruiting bodies.
seasonality.summer: During dry summer periods, the lichen often appears more grayish and may seem less prominent. The crusty texture becomes more noticeable when dry.
seasonality.fall: Fall rains can bring out the greenish tones again, and the lichen may appear more vibrant against autumn bark colors.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round on bark, often easier to spot against snow-covered backgrounds. Winter moisture can enhance the greenish coloration.

funFact: This lichen can actually help clean the air around it by absorbing pollutants, and scientists use lichens like this one as natural air quality monitors - the healthier the lichen community, the cleaner the air!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other crusty gray lichens on bark, but the combination of its gray-green color, button-like dark fruiting bodies, and preference for smooth bark in well-lit areas helps distinguish it. Remember: if it's crusty, gray-green, and has obvious dark 'buttons,' you're likely looking at a Buellia species.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that lichens aren't plants at all, but rather a remarkable partnership between fungi and algae (or cyanobacteria) that has evolved to work so well together that we give them a single name. This cooperation allows lichens to colonize surfaces where neither partner could survive alone.
compareHints: Compared to Common Button Lichen (Buellia erubescens), this species tends to have a more greenish cast rather than pure gray coloration. Unlike Sunken Button Lichen (Buellia spuria), the fruiting bodies of B. griseovirens sit more prominently on the surface rather than appearing sunken into the lichen body. The gray-green color shift with moisture is more pronounced in this species than in its close relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Common Button Lichen differs from its Buellia relatives by being the most widespread and found at the broadest range of elevations.

Sunken Button Lichen stands out from its Button Lichen relatives by having the most dramatic black-and-white contrast - the black borders are much more prominent and continuous than in Common Button Lichen.
Unlike Common Button Lichen which has a more uniform gray surface, Speckled Button Lichen is distinguished by its characteristic spotted pattern.
